newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. limps along by not paying peacekeepers.
newsitem.headline: U.N. limps along by not paying peacekeepers.

text.p: The United Nations, in debt for more than $2 billion, is limping along by not paying states, such as France and Britain, who contributed troops to peacekeeping ventures, its chief financial officer said on Tuesday.
"One group of member states finances another," said Joseph Connor, the undersecretary-general for administration and management, at a press conference on the U.N. budget.

Because of a continuing shortfall for day-to-day expenses, mainly because of the U.S. debt of more than $1 billion, the United Nations has to borrow from peacekeeping funds, which means not paying those contributing troops.

Highest on the list is France, owed about $135 million, followed by Britain at about $80 million. The Netherlands, Pakistan and India come next, followed by nearly every country that has contributed troops to the United Nations since 1990.

Connor, the former chief executive officer of the Price Waterhouse accounting firm, emphasised President Bill Clinton's proposed $1 billion payment for arrears was really only $712 million for peacekeeping and regular dues.
The remainder included in the U.S. president's $1,021 billion package of arrears included contributions to U.N. specialised agencies and other international organisations.
But conservatives in Congress are far from approving the monies unless the world body first severely streamlines its bureaucracy and abolishes many of its programmes.

If the money were allocated, Connor said a U.S. debt of $362 million would remain, mainly because of Washington's unilateral reduction of 5 percent to 25 percent on peacekeeping expenses, which the United Nations does not recognise.
Borrowing from peacekeeping to keep up operating expenses has ranged from $200 million to $300 million each year. Connor estimated the figure would be about $225 million by the end of 1997.

Most of the arrears date from 1993-94 when peacekeeping expanded to nearly 80,000 troops because of large operations in Cambodia, Somalia and Bosnia, all running at the same time. Currently, the number of peacekeepers has fallen to 25,000 and is expected to be reduced further.
But Connor said this made little difference in financing past and present peacekeeping operations as long as the debts were not paid.

He also predicted further unspecified belt tightening at the United Nations over the next several years, even before any promised reforms or restructuring take place. About 1,000 jobs were left vacant over the past two years and further unspecified cuts would probably have to be made.

Connor's statement also illustrated the financial dependency of the United Nations on the United States. Both the Clinton administration and the Congress want to reduce this by putting a cap of 20 percent on regular dues and 25 percent for peacekeeping ventures.
But so far Europeans and Japan, who pick up most of the bills, are reluctant to make any concessions to Washington until they believe substantial progress would be made on the current arrears.
"The United States has not a positive record regarding implementing previous agreements to pay U.S. arrears," said Jan Berteling of the Netherlands, representing the European Union.
